title: Your Agent Evolved. Your Evals Didn't. — Ameya Bhatawdekar, Braintrust
talk_summary: The speaker argues that as agent architectures evolve with model capabilities, evals must evolve too, moving from final-answer checks to node-level and distributional evals. He recommends a production-data flywheel that harvests failures and clusters them to discover new failure modes, using pass@k/pass^k to separate capability from reliability.

takeaways.technique: pass@k and pass^k for agent reliability
takeaways.what_they_do: Run the same eval k times; pass@k checks whether it succeeds at least once, while pass^k measures how often all k runs succeed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: pass at K is like if you take the same that eval and you run it K times does it succeed at least once

takeaways.what_they_do: Evaluate each orchestration node and handoff contract in addition to the end-to-end result, because failures can occur in parsing, retrieval, tool calls, or branch logic.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you have to have node level evals

takeaways.what_they_do: Treat model swaps as architecture changes: re-run evals for each candidate model because old prompts/tool logic may encode assumptions from prior model limits.
takeaways.evidence_quote: architecture follows model updates and your evals have to follow your architecture

takeaways.technique: golden defect set for LLM PR reviewer
takeaways.what_they_do: Build a golden dataset that encodes what good and bad outputs look like, then score the reviewer against it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: put together a golden data set

takeaways.what_they_do: Harvest production traces and cluster them to surface unanticipated failure categories, then turn those clusters into new eval cases.
takeaways.evidence_quote: find new categories of failures that you had not anticipated

takeaways.what_they_do: Automate eval runs as part of the workflow so changes are checked against durable eval assets.
takeaways.evidence_quote: robust eval discipline uh with the right tools and the right automation
